question: Does this survey give a precise, comprehensive, and empirically grounded account of how neural-network knowledge can be edited reliably, generally, locally, and efficiently across edit regimes and domains, and which parts of its taxonomy and evidence remain valid under current benchmarks?

key_findings.claim: The survey's most useful contribution is a domain-independent operational framework that separates what must change, what must remain stable, and whether edits arrive singly, in batches, or over time.
key_findings.evidence: The paper defines an edit as an input-output correction to a fixed-task model, distinguishes single and batched edits from successive and non-successive edits, and asks an editor to change edit behavior while preserving other behavior. This vocabulary is compact enough to compare work from computer vision, natural-language processing, safety repair, and graph learning, and the explicit inclusion of efficiency is practically important because avoiding full retraining is the premise of editing.

anchors.section: Section 2.1 and Figure 1, background and four edit regimes
Sections 2.2-2.3, operational definition and edit taxonomy

key_findings.claim: The framework measures changed behavior, not whether a model's internal knowledge representation was identified or causally rewritten.
key_findings.evidence: Success is defined by the edited function returning a requested output and preserving outputs elsewhere. No internal proposition, representation, causal pathway, consistency closure, or epistemic state must be identified. Weight edits, auxiliary memories, routers, patches, and ordinary constrained fine-tuning can therefore all satisfy the same interface despite making fundamentally different changes. Calling every successful behavioral intervention a knowledge update is a useful convention, but it is not evidence that a localized item of knowledge existed or was edited.

anchors.section: Section 2.2, formal model and editor definition

key_findings.claim: Reliability, generality, locality, and efficiency form a valuable checklist, but the paper leaves the decisive generalization neighborhood and locality domain benchmark-defined and under-specified.
key_findings.evidence: Generality requires the target output over an equivalence neighborhood N(x_e), while locality requires unchanged labels outside it. The paper does not prescribe how to construct that neighborhood or cover paraphrases, aliases, related facts, temporal context, logical consequences, multi-hop questions, multilingual variants, or downstream tasks. A method's measured generality and locality can consequently change substantially with the evaluator's chosen probes even when the editor is unchanged.

anchors.section: Section 2.5, retain metrics and task transition

key_findings.claim: The formalization contains several visible notation errors, including a reversed function-space exponent, a self-bound generality variable, and an ill-indexed combined edit-success metric.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 1 prints F := (X x Theta)^Y even though the prose defines parameterized maps from X x Theta to Y; standard function-space notation would reverse that exponent or use an arrow. Equation 7 states the condition for all x_e in N(x_e) while the left side uses a perturbed input, rather than quantifying the perturbed variable. In Equation 12 the first component is averaged over edit indices n and b, but the second sums only an i index, leaving n and b free and failing to express the stated average of paraphrase generalization over edits. These are repairable notation defects, but they weaken a survey whose common formal framework is a central contribution.

key_findings.claim: The proposed locality metrics are too weak to establish that an edit is behaviorally contained.
key_findings.evidence: Locality is formalized as exact preservation of selected labels, and Drawdown is an accuracy ratio on a test set. Both can miss large probability or logit changes that do not flip the top label, calibration damage, generation fluency, contradictions, safety changes, reasoning degradation, and failures on unrelated tasks. The survey briefly mentions fluency and consistency as domain-specific additions, but neither the general metric suite nor its comparison table operationalizes broad collateral harm.

anchors.section: Table 4, SR, GR, and DD comparison

key_findings.claim: The task and dataset inventory usefully broadens model editing beyond factual language-model updates, but it also contains factual and typographic errors.
key_findings.evidence: Sections 3.1-3.3 cover image classification and inpainting, fact checking, closed-book question answering, text generation and classification, formal repair of ACAS Xu controllers, and graph-node editing. However, Table 1 reports 600k CIFAR-100 examples although CIFAR-100 contains 60k images, and Table 2 reports 120M zsRE examples although the original zsRE paper reports more than 30M reading-comprehension examples. CounterFact is also misspelled as ConterFact in Table 4. These errors make the dataset tables unsafe as a source of record without checking the primary papers.

key_findings.claim: Many surveyed benchmarks inject arbitrary labels or counterfactual triples, so they test targeted behavior injection more directly than truthful, temporally grounded knowledge correction.
key_findings.evidence: The computer-vision and fact-checking descriptions include randomly relabeled examples or flipped labels, while ROME-style factual editing relies on CounterFact's counterfactual assertions. These settings are convenient because edit targets and paraphrases can be generated automatically, but they do not establish whether a model incorporates a real-world update coherently across context, temporal qualifiers, multi-hop consequences, related relations, or downstream decisions. Conflating finite factual edits with hallucination mitigation similarly overstates what these tests measure.

anchors.section: Section 3.2, fact-checking and question-answering edit construction
Section 3.2, text generation and factual editing

key_findings.claim: The four method families are readable navigation aids but not mutually exclusive or conceptually orthogonal categories.
key_findings.evidence: Regularization and meta-learning describe optimization mechanisms, direct model editing describes the locus or form of an intervention, and architectural strategies describe deployment structure. A hypernetwork directly changes weights; a memory-and-router architecture is trained and can use regularization; direct editors often depend on localization models or causal analysis. Table 3 therefore records editorial assignments across overlapping axes rather than a partition from which comparative conclusions follow.

key_findings.claim: Table 3's capability and large-model scaling checkmarks are not supported by a transparent extraction rule and are internally inconsistent with the survey's own descriptions.
key_findings.evidence: The paper defines a large model as having more than 10B parameters, yet marks ROME as scaling to large models even though the cited ROME evaluation used GPT-J 6B and smaller models. It also marks MALMEN as scaling despite the cited evaluations reaching GPT-J 6B and T5-XL 2.8B, and marks KnowledgeEditor despite BERT/BART experiments plus an auxiliary hypernetwork. No citation, model size, uncertainty, or decision rule is attached to individual cells, and a check can variously mean demonstrated, claimed, or believed possible.

anchors.section: Section 4 and Table 3, capability matrix and >10B definition
Figure 2 and transition to direct editing
Section 4.3, ROME and MEMIT model scales

key_findings.claim: The survey runs no original experiment, and its quantitative comparison is too narrow to rank editing approaches generally.
key_findings.evidence: Table 4 explicitly adapts results from Yao et al. for one GPT-J 6B model, two factual datasets, and non-sequential batch editing; Figure 2 is adapted from MEMIT. The survey reports no rerun, matched hyperparameters, compute budget, seeds, confidence interval, statistical test, or cross-domain replication. Consequently the numbers describe one inherited setup and cannot establish which method is best across the four edit regimes, model families, domains, or collateral effects represented elsewhere in the survey.

anchors.section: End of Section 4, qualitative method summaries

key_findings.claim: Later primary evaluations expose evaluation axes omitted by the survey and show that high single-edit benchmark scores can coexist with poor logical propagation, broad ability damage, and sequential collapse.
key_findings.evidence: MQuAKE evaluates multi-hop consequences; RippleEdits tests logical ripple effects across 5,000 edits and finds prominent editors weak, with in-context editing strongest in its study. Scale audits report gradual and catastrophic forgetting and damage to unrelated general abilities. Mirage's realistic QAEdit and WILD settings report 38.5% single-edit performance versus previously reported 96.8%, identify teacher-forcing leakage, and observe failure by 1,000 sequential edits. Cross-lingual and multimodal benchmarks add aliases, languages, modality consistency, and robustness. These results do not invalidate the survey's four desiderata; they show that its concrete probes substantially under-instantiate them.

key_findings.claim: The review is narrative rather than systematic, so its claim to cover the most relevant approaches cannot be independently reproduced or audited for selection bias.
key_findings.evidence: The paper supplies no searched databases, search strings, dates or cutoff, inclusion and exclusion criteria, duplicate-removal process, screened and included counts, quality appraisal, extraction template, reviewer agreement, or released bibliography corpus. Method selection and Table 3 labels are therefore not reproducible. This is especially consequential in a fast-moving field where an earlier same-year LLM editing survey and benchmark is cited but not positioned as a competing survey.

key_findings.claim: The broad 'first work' priority claim is not defensible, although the survey appears broader across task domains than the earlier LLM-focused review.
key_findings.evidence: The introduction describes this as the first effort to categorize editing methods, formalize the problem, and provide comprehensive analysis. Yao et al.'s Editing Large Language Models: Problems, Methods, and Opportunities was submitted in May 2023, before this survey's October 2023 submission, and already presents an LLM-editing overview, method taxonomy, empirical benchmark, dataset, and toolkit. This survey does add computer vision, formal repair, graph editing, and wider neighboring-field coverage, so a defensible claim is first or early cross-domain synthesis rather than first knowledge-editing survey generally.

anchors.section: Section 4, mention of the Yao et al. comparative study

key_findings.claim: The discussion of malicious editing and ethical correction identifies an important frontier but does not yet constitute a security or governance protocol.
key_findings.evidence: The paper warns that editors can implant backdoors, vulnerabilities, hidden behavior, or harmful tendencies and calls for edit verification and ethical guidelines. It does not define authorized editors, a threat model, provenance, rollback, audit logs, integrity protection, adversarial edit detection, red-team tests, dispute handling, or metrics for plural values. The section is therefore a useful risk agenda rather than evidence that current editors can be deployed safely or that 'ethical editing' has an agreed target.

method.core_idea: Unify neural-network editing as a behavior-preserving model transformation, organize edit requests along batch and sequence axes, evaluate four desired properties, and synthesize methods into four broad families across several application domains.
method.mechanism: The survey defines a starting function f0, one or more edit pairs, and a knowledge-editing transformation that produces an edited function. It enumerates single versus batched and successive versus non-successive regimes; translates reliability, generality, locality, and efficiency into success, generalization, drawdown, and retain metrics; inventories tasks and datasets; and narratively groups prior work into regularization, meta-learning or hypernetwork, direct-weight, and architectural or memory strategies. It then relates editing to unlearning, continual learning, and parameter-efficient tuning and proposes future directions. Evidence consists of cited studies, four summary tables, and two adapted figures; the authors run no new experiment or systematic-review protocol.
assumptions: A desired model correction can be specified by one or more input-output pairs from the same task as the base model.
Behavior on a finite edit set and evaluator-defined variants is a sufficient proxy for changing the intended knowledge.
The equivalence neighborhood around an edit and the locality set outside it can be constructed faithfully for each domain.
Preserving exact predictions or aggregate task accuracy captures the collateral behavior that users care about.
Reliability, generality, locality, and efficiency transfer meaningfully across classification, generation, formal repair, and graph tasks.
The four method families provide a useful comparison even though mechanism, intervention locus, and deployment architecture overlap.
Results adapted across papers remain comparable despite differences in implementation, hyperparameters, compute, model state, and evaluator construction.
Counterfactual and randomly relabeled benchmarks are informative proxies for realistic factual correction and changing-world updates.
Cited work selected narratively is representative enough to support field-level conclusions without a reproducible search and screening protocol.

techniques.role: Crosses edit batch size with sequentiality to define four operational evaluation regimes.
Represents editing as a transformation from a base function and requested input-output changes to an edited function.
Uses reliability, generality, locality, and efficiency as the survey's common desiderata.
Adds final-model success and generalization retention measures for successive edits.
Maps editing formulations and datasets across vision, language, safety verification, and graph learning.
Groups methods into regularization, meta-learning or hypernetwork, direct-weight, and architectural or memory families.
Summarizes training requirements, architecture changes, extra data, edit regimes, and claimed large-model scalability.
Compares editing with machine unlearning, continual learning, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
Identifies scaling, introspection, cross-domain benchmarks, runtime and multimodal editing, fairness, and verification as open directions.

evaluations.metric: Reliability, generality, locality, efficiency, and retain-rate definitions.
evaluations.result: The paper gives a compact common interface and metric vocabulary, but Equations 1, 7, and 12 contain notation or indexing errors and the evaluator-defined neighborhoods remain under-specified.
evaluations.baseline: Prior papers' heterogeneous definitions of patching, efficacy, specificity, paraphrase generalization, and sequential editing.

evaluations.baseline: LLM-only editing surveys and the individual task papers.

limitations: Author-stated: knowledge editing is recent and lacks a clear definition, common task description, and consolidated repository of work.
Author-stated: current approaches face scaling, introspection, cross-domain benchmarking, runtime adaptation, multimodal extension, robustness, fairness, and dual-use challenges.
Reviewer-identified: behavior-level edit success does not demonstrate that an internal fact or causal knowledge representation was localized and rewritten.
Reviewer-identified: equivalence neighborhoods and locality sets are not operationally standardized, making generality and specificity scores benchmark-dependent.
Reviewer-identified: exact-label preservation and aggregate accuracy Drawdown miss probability drift, calibration, reasoning, safety, fluency, contradiction, and unrelated-task damage.
Reviewer-identified: the four-family taxonomy mixes optimization mechanism, intervention locus, and deployment architecture, so categories overlap.
Reviewer-identified: the capability matrix has no cell-level provenance or uncertainty and conflicts with its stated >10B scaling threshold in several entries.

Reviewer-identified: all numerical results and scaling curves are adapted from cited work; no independent experiment, seed variation, confidence interval, compute normalization, or statistical test is provided.
Reviewer-identified: dataset tables contain factual and typographic errors and emphasize synthetic label flips and counterfactual facts over realistic temporal and logical updates.
Reviewer-identified: no systematic search, cutoff, screening, inclusion criterion, extraction protocol, quality appraisal, reviewer agreement, or reusable literature corpus is reported.
Reviewer-identified: the first-survey claim is too broad because Yao et al.'s earlier 2023 LLM editing survey and benchmark already covers problems, methods, and opportunities.
Reviewer-identified: security and ethical editing are discussed normatively without an authorization model, audit and rollback system, adversarial evaluation, or plural-value governance.
failure_modes: Declaring an edit general because it succeeds on a small paraphrase list while failing on aliases, contextual variants, other languages, multi-hop consequences, or related facts.
Declaring an edit local because top-one labels remain unchanged even though probabilities, calibration, reasoning, generation quality, safety, or downstream tasks degrade.
Treating a counterfactual prompt-target association as evidence that a coherent proposition was causally rewritten inside model parameters.
Comparing methods across papers without controlling the base checkpoint, edit order, batch size, optimizer, prompts, evaluator, compute, and retained-edit horizon.
Inferring large-model scalability from a successful 6B experiment or from asymptotic plausibility without a size and edit-horizon scaling curve.
Using random label flips or false triples as a proxy for changing-world knowledge and overlooking truth provenance, time, ambiguity, and contradiction closure.
Applying a single edit repeatedly until it passes and hiding teacher-forcing, evaluator leakage, selection bias, or failures accumulated across prior edits.
Calling a memory router and a weight editor equivalent because both pass the same immediate output test while ignoring latency, storage, retrievability, rollback, and failure isolation.
Using editing to suppress hallucination without testing open-ended generation, source attribution, abstention, consistency, and newly introduced false claims.
Authorizing automated ethical edits under a single scalar target that can be gamed or can erase legitimate, contested, or context-dependent behavior.
Publishing a narrative method table whose checkmarks silently combine demonstrated capability, author claim, and reviewer expectation.
reusable_insights: Evaluate edit systems on a grid spanning edit batch size, sequential horizon, model scale, domain, and intervention type rather than reporting one aggregate success score.
Separate behavioral correction, representational change, factual truth, logical propagation, and downstream utility; an editor can succeed on one and fail on the others.
Define edit neighborhoods as versioned test generators covering paraphrases, aliases, relation reversals, temporal qualifiers, multilingual forms, multi-hop consequences, and adversarial contexts.
Measure locality at multiple levels: exact output, distribution shift, calibration, generation quality, broad capabilities, safety behavior, and unrelated tasks.
Replace the four exclusive families with composable axes such as edit target, update mechanism, storage locus, retrieval or routing, train-time dependency, persistence, and rollback.
Attach primary-source evidence, model size, edit regime, confidence, and a demonstrated-versus-claimed flag to every capability-matrix cell.
Validate scaling along both model size and edit horizon; a method that works once on a larger model may still collapse under many edits, and a small-model success need not extrapolate.
Use realistic, timestamped updates with provenance and known relational consequences alongside counterfactual stress tests, then score both immediate correction and consistency closure.
Report matched compute, memory, latency, storage growth, seeds, confidence intervals, base-model checkpoints, edit order, and evaluator leakage controls.
For deployable editing, make authorization, provenance, audit logs, diff inspection, rollback, conflict resolution, and adversarial verification first-class modules.
A cross-domain survey remains valuable even when evidence cannot be pooled, but its corpus discovery, screening, extraction, and taxonomy decisions should be reproducible.
open_questions: What observable evidence can distinguish a coherent knowledge update from a local input-output patch or a retrieved exception?
How can equivalence neighborhoods and logical ripple sets be generated with high recall without leaking the edit target or rewarding superficial lexical matching?
Which locality probes predict real deployment harm better than exact-label agreement or aggregate task accuracy?
Can a factorial benchmark independently vary model size, number and order of edits, relation complexity, modality, language, and evaluator reliability at tractable cost?
Which scaling curves or mechanistic diagnostics can justify extrapolation from a small edited model to a substantially larger one before the full experiment is affordable?
When do sequential editors fail gradually, catastrophically, or through router interference, and can an online monitor predict the transition before broad abilities collapse?
How should conflicts between new edits, previous edits, model priors, retrieved evidence, and time-indexed facts be represented and resolved?
Can realistic update benchmarks separate source-grounded truth correction from malicious or merely counterfactual behavior injection?
What minimum set of cross-domain tests would support the claim that an editing mechanism generalizes beyond factual language-model associations?
How should edit verification combine causal tracing, behavior suites, integrity checks, provenance, human review, and reversible deployment?
Which value judgments in safety or ethical editing can be automated, and which require accountable human authorization and appeal?
Can a living systematic review preserve primary-source revision provenance while keeping a fast-moving editing taxonomy and result matrix current?

competitive_landscape.title: Editing Large Language Models: Problems, Methods, and Opportunities
competitive_landscape.difference: Yao and colleagues submitted an LLM-focused editing survey before this paper, organized problems and methods, independently benchmarked representative approaches, introduced a dataset, and released the EasyEdit toolkit. The present survey is broader across vision, safety repair, and graph learning, but its unqualified first-survey claim and lack of original benchmark are weakened by this predecessor.

competitive_landscape.title: EasyEdit: An Easy-to-use Knowledge Editing Framework for Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: EasyEdit turns a related survey taxonomy into a modular implementation, evaluation framework, documentation, and runnable support for multiple editors and LLMs. This survey provides wider conceptual scope, while EasyEdit supplies the executable artifact and common experimental surface that its narrative comparison lacks.

competitive_landscape.title: MQuAKE: Assessing Knowledge Editing in Language Models via Multi-Hop Questions
competitive_landscape.difference: MQuAKE tests whether edited facts propagate through multi-hop questions, exposing failures that paraphrase-level generality cannot see. It operationalizes a consequence neighborhood absent from the survey's SR, GR, and Drawdown presentation, though it remains language-model and QA specific.

competitive_landscape.title: Evaluating the Ripple Effects of Knowledge Editing in Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: RippleEdits supplies 5,000 edits and probes logical, compositional, and contextual consequences, finding prominent parameter editors weak and in-context editing strongest in its evaluation. It gives concrete content to the survey's under-specified generality neighborhood and shows why immediate edit and paraphrase success are insufficient.

competitive_landscape.title: WISE: Rethinking the Knowledge Memory for Lifelong Model Editing of Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: WISE separates a main memory from a side memory, routes edited knowledge, and shards updates to address lifelong editing and the tension among reliability, generalization, and locality. It exemplifies why mechanism, storage locus, and routing are more informative composable axes than assigning a method only to the survey's architectural family.

competitive_landscape.title: AlphaEdit: Null-Space Constrained Knowledge Editing for Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: AlphaEdit projects updates into a null space intended to preserve prior knowledge and targets sequential editing performance. It is a direct methodological successor to ROME and MEMIT-style weight writing, while later reproducibility work indicates that architecture, horizon, fluency, broad-capability, and safety limits still require tests beyond immediate benchmark scores.

competitive_landscape.title: Model Editing at Scale leads to Gradual and Catastrophic Forgetting
competitive_landscape.difference: Gupta and colleagues show that repeated ROME and MEMIT edits can first degrade gradually and then catastrophically, damaging editability and downstream performance. Their horizon-level audit turns the survey's successive-edit retention property into a failure trajectory and challenges conclusions drawn from single or short-batch edits.

competitive_landscape.title: Model Editing Harms General Abilities of Large Language Models: Regularization to the Rescue
competitive_landscape.difference: Gu and colleagues evaluate four editors, three LLMs, and eight general tasks, finding that edits can harm broad capabilities and proposing RECT regularization. The work demonstrates a locality failure invisible to the survey's selected-label and Drawdown framing and provides a broader task panel for collateral effects.

competitive_landscape.title: The Mirage of Model Editing: Revisiting Evaluation in the Wild
competitive_landscape.difference: Mirage introduces QAEdit and WILD, reports 38.5% single-edit performance versus previously reported 96.8%, identifies teacher-forcing leakage, and finds failure at 1,000 sequential edits. It directly challenges the validity of clean synthetic evaluation regimes summarized in the survey and emphasizes realistic prompts and leakage-resistant scoring.

competitive_landscape.title: Lifelong Knowledge Editing for LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Continuous Prompt Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: RECIPE combines a retriever, continuous prompts, and a sentinel mechanism for lifelong edits instead of repeatedly overwriting base weights. It supplies an architectural alternative whose storage growth, routing, rollback, and latency tradeoffs should be compared separately from parametric edit success.

competitive_landscape.title: BabelEdits: A Benchmark and a Modular Approach for Robust Cross-lingual Knowledge Editing of Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: BabelEdits evaluates edits across 60 languages, includes alias variation, and studies downstream degradation, making linguistic transfer an explicit generality axis. It extends far beyond the survey's mostly English paraphrase neighborhood and motivates modular evaluation of editing and multilingual retrieval or routing.

competitive_landscape.title: Editing the Moving World: Model Editing for Video LLMs
competitive_landscape.difference: This work introduces a video-LLM editing benchmark spanning reliability, locality, generality, and robustness, operationalizing the multimodal future direction that the survey only proposes. Temporal visual evidence adds cross-frame and cross-modal consistency obligations absent from text-fact and static-image benchmarks.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The introduction presents the work as the first effort to categorize knowledge-editing methods, formalize the problem, comprehensively analyze approaches and datasets, distinguish the field from adjacent research, and outline future opportunities.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Sections 2-3 provide a cross-domain edit framework, four-regime taxonomy, property and metric definitions, and task inventory; Section 4 organizes methods into four families with qualitative and inherited quantitative comparisons; Section 5 connects neighboring fields and risks. The paper's own Table 4 is adapted from Yao et al., whose LLM editing survey and benchmark was submitted months earlier in 2023.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is an early and unusually broad cross-domain synthesis, especially its explicit batch-by-sequence edit grid, efficiency desideratum, inclusion of vision, formal repair, and graph learning, and links to unlearning and parameter-efficient tuning. It is not the first knowledge-editing survey generally, its four families overlap, its central formalization has notation defects, and its evidence base is neither systematic nor independently empirical. Current value lies in the conceptual scaffold, which should be rebuilt as a reproducible, multi-axis living review with cell-level provenance and modern logical, sequential, realistic, multilingual, multimodal, ability, and security evaluations.

reviewer_notes: Read all 24 pages of the exact archived PDF revision, including equations, footnotes, and the complete bibliography. Rendered every page at 120 dpi in RGB and visually inspected both figures, all four tables, formal notation, captions, and reference pages; no visually encoded evidence was omitted. The audit checked twelve current primary related-work records on 2026-08-23, spanning the earlier LLM survey and toolkit, multi-hop and ripple-effect benchmarks, lifelong parametric and retrieval-based editors, sequential forgetting, broad-capability harm, realistic leakage-resistant evaluation, cross-lingual transfer, and video editing. Dataset counts were checked against their primary records. The article reports no original experiment, code, literature-search log, screened-paper corpus, extraction form, or statistical analysis; its numerical table and scaling figure are explicitly adapted from cited work.
